::: {.solutions}

Ten proofs whose lines have been jumbled. For each, **anchor the ends** (the "Let/Suppose/Assume" line
first, the conclusion last), then order the middle so **every line is justified by the ones above it**.
These mirror the Paper 2 **Prf4** multiple-choice format.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Method.** first line = *Let / Suppose / Assume* or the given · last line = the conclusion (or "… a
contradiction, so …") · middle = follow the dependencies ("$a=2c$" only after "$a$ is even").
:::

---

## Question 1

::: {.question}
The following prove "the sum of two even numbers is even." Which ordering is correct?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(i)** So the sum is $2(a+b)$, which is even. &nbsp;&nbsp; **(ii)** Let the two even numbers be
$2a$ and $2b$. &nbsp;&nbsp; **(iii)** Their sum is $2a+2b$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** (ii),(iii),(i) &nbsp; **B** (ii),(i),(iii) &nbsp; **C** (iii),(ii),(i) &nbsp;
**D** (i),(ii),(iii)
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(Easy — direct)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**A.** (ii) is the opening "Let…"; (i) is the conclusion "…even"; (iii) is the algebra between them, since
(i)'s $2(a+b)$ comes from (iii)'s $2a+2b$. $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3.5cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 2

::: {.question}
Order the proof of "if $n$ is odd, then $n^2$ is odd."

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(i)** Then $n^2=(2k+1)^2=4k^2+4k+1$. &nbsp;&nbsp; **(ii)** Let $n=2k+1$. &nbsp;&nbsp;
**(iii)** So $n^2=2(2k^2+2k)+1$, which is odd.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** (ii),(i),(iii) &nbsp; **B** (i),(ii),(iii) &nbsp; **C** (ii),(iii),(i) &nbsp;
**D** (iii),(i),(ii)
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(Easy → Medium — direct)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**A.** Open with $n=2k+1$ (ii); square it (i); rearrange to $2(\dots)+1$ (iii). (iii) needs (i)'s
expansion first. $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3.5cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 3

::: {.question}
Order the proof of "$n^2+n$ is even for every integer $n$."

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(i)** If $n$ is even, $n=2k$, then $n^2+n=2(2k^2+k)$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(ii)** In both cases $n^2+n$ is even, so it holds for all $n$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(iii)** Every integer is even or odd.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(iv)** If $n$ is odd, $n=2k+1$, then $n^2+n=2(2k^2+3k+1)$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** (iii),(i),(iv),(ii) &nbsp; **B** (i),(iv),(iii),(ii) &nbsp; **C** (iii),(ii),(i),(iv)
&nbsp; **D** (i),(iii),(iv),(ii)
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(Medium — cases)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**A.** State the exhaustive split (iii) first; do each case (i),(iv); conclude (ii) — which refers to
"both cases", so it must come **after** them. $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 4

::: {.question}
Order the proof of "there is no largest positive integer."

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(i)** Then $N+1$ is a positive integer larger than $N$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(ii)** Suppose there is a largest positive integer, $N$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(iii)** This contradicts $N$ being the largest, so no largest exists.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** (ii),(i),(iii) &nbsp; **B** (i),(ii),(iii) &nbsp; **C** (ii),(iii),(i) &nbsp;
**D** (iii),(ii),(i)
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(Medium — contradiction)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**A.** Assume the opposite (ii); derive the larger integer (i); state the contradiction and conclude
(iii). $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3.5cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 5

::: {.question}
Order the proof of "a rational plus an irrational is irrational."

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(i)** Then $i=s-r$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(ii)** Suppose $r+i=s$ is rational, where $r$ is rational and $i$ is irrational.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(iii)** But a difference of two rationals is rational, so $i$ would be rational — a
contradiction.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(iv)** Hence $r+i$ is irrational.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** (ii),(i),(iii),(iv) &nbsp; **B** (ii),(iii),(i),(iv) &nbsp; **C** (i),(ii),(iii),(iv)
&nbsp; **D** (ii),(i),(iv),(iii)
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(Medium → Hard — contradiction)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**A.** Assume the sum rational (ii); solve for $i$ (i); reach the contradiction (iii) — which needs (i)
first; conclude (iv). $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 6

::: {.question}
Order the disproof of "every prime number is odd."

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(i)** But $2$ is even. &nbsp;&nbsp; **(ii)** Consider the number $2$, which is prime.
&nbsp;&nbsp; **(iii)** So not every prime is odd.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** (ii),(i),(iii) &nbsp; **B** (i),(ii),(iii) &nbsp; **C** (ii),(iii),(i) &nbsp;
**D** (iii),(ii),(i)
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(Easy — counterexample)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**A.** Name the counterexample (ii); show it breaks the claim (i); conclude the claim is false (iii).
$\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 7

::: {.question}
Order the proof of "the product of two consecutive integers is even."

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(i)** One of two consecutive integers is even.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(ii)** Let the integers be $n$ and $n+1$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(iii)** So their product $n(n+1)$ has an even factor, hence is even.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** (ii),(i),(iii) &nbsp; **B** (i),(ii),(iii) &nbsp; **C** (ii),(iii),(i) &nbsp;
**D** (i),(iii),(ii)
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(Medium — direct)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**A.** Introduce the integers (ii); note one is even (i); conclude the product is even (iii).
$\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 8

::: {.question}
Order the proof of "$\sqrt3$ is irrational" (you may use: if $3$ divides $a^2$ then $3$ divides $a$).

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(i)** Suppose $\sqrt3=\dfrac ab$ in lowest terms.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(ii)** Then $a^2=3b^2$, so $3$ divides $a^2$, hence $3$ divides $a$; write $a=3c$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(iii)** So $9c^2=3b^2$, i.e. $b^2=3c^2$, so $3$ divides $b$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(iv)** But then $a$ and $b$ share the factor $3$ — a contradiction.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(v)** Therefore $\sqrt3$ is irrational.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** (i),(ii),(iii),(iv),(v) &nbsp; **B** (i),(iii),(ii),(iv),(v) &nbsp;
**C** (ii),(i),(iii),(v),(iv) &nbsp; **D** (i),(ii),(iv),(iii),(v)
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(Hard — contradiction)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**A.** Assume lowest terms (i); get "$3$ divides $a$" and $a=3c$ (ii); substitute to get "$3$ divides $b$" (iii) — this
**needs** $a=3c$ from (ii); the shared factor is the contradiction (iv); conclude (v). $\;\blacksquare$

*The trap is (iii) before (ii): you cannot use $a=3c$ before deriving it.*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4.5cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 9

::: {.question}
This proof of "if $n^2$ is even then $n$ is even" (by contrapositive) has its lines listed as
**(1),(2),(3),(4)** — but **one line is in the wrong place**.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(1)** Suppose $n$ is odd.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(2)** So $n^2$ is odd, proving the contrapositive.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(3)** Then $n=2k+1$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(4)** So $n^2=(2k+1)^2=2(2k^2+2k)+1$.

What is the correct order?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** (1),(3),(4),(2) &nbsp; **B** (1),(2),(3),(4) &nbsp; **C** (3),(1),(4),(2) &nbsp;
**D** (1),(4),(3),(2)
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(Hard — one line is misplaced)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**A.** Line (2) is the **conclusion**, so it must come **last** — it was misplaced at position 2. Correct:
suppose $n$ odd (1), write $n=2k+1$ (3), square it (4), conclude $n^2$ odd (2). $\;\blacksquare$

*A conclusion line ("So … proving …") can never sit in the middle.*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 10

::: {.question}
Order the proof of "the product of any three consecutive integers is divisible by $6$."

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(i)** Among three consecutive integers, one is a multiple of $2$ and one is a multiple of $3$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(ii)** Let the integers be $n,\,n+1,\,n+2$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(iii)** So the product is divisible by both $2$ and $3$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(iv)** Since $2$ and $3$ are coprime, the product is divisible by $6$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** (ii),(i),(iii),(iv) &nbsp; **B** (i),(ii),(iii),(iv) &nbsp; **C** (ii),(iii),(i),(iv)
&nbsp; **D** (ii),(i),(iv),(iii)
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(Hard — longer direct proof)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**A.** Introduce the integers (ii); note the multiples of $2$ and $3$ (i); deduce divisibility by both
(iii); combine via coprimality to get $6$ (iv). $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}
Working
:::

---

::: {.callout-tip}
## The one habit to leave with

**Anchor the ends first** — the "Let / Suppose / Assume" line opens, the conclusion (or contradiction)
closes — then order the middle by **dependency**: a line that uses a result must come after it. A
conclusion line is never in the middle.
:::

:::
